title: Short Replies with Auxiliary Verbs
summary: Give concise answers and contrasts without repeating a complete verb phrase. Choose the auxiliary that matches the tense or modal in the first part of the sentence.
learningObjectives: Use a suitable auxiliary in a short contrasting statement instead of repeating words.
Give affirmative and negative short answers with be, have, do and modal verbs.
Choose do/does for present simple and did for past simple statements.
Avoid leaving affirmative contracted forms alone at the end of a short reply.

explanation.heading: An auxiliary can replace the rest of an idea
explanation.body: When a verb phrase is already clear, repeat only its helping verb in a second clause. This works with forms of be, have, do and modal verbs such as can, will and might. The omitted words are understood from the earlier clause.
explanation.example: I can't skate, but my sister can.

explanation.heading: Match the verb and time
explanation.body: Use am/is/are for present be, was/were for past be, and have/has when those verbs form a perfect phrase. For present simple action verbs, use do or does; for past simple, use did. Match the subject: he does, they do, she has.
explanation.example: Ella visited the market on Sunday, but we didn't.

explanation.heading: Yes and no short answers
explanation.body: A short answer usually repeats the auxiliary from the question with the correct subject. Yes, I am; No, she isn't; Yes, we have; No, he can't; Yes, they will. Use do/does/did when the question is in the simple present or past without be.

explanation.heading: Negative forms are useful in contrasts
explanation.body: Negative forms such as don't, doesn't, didn't, isn't, haven't and won't can stand at the end of a clause. They often make a contrast clear without repeating the whole action. Use the tense from the earlier information.
explanation.example: The children have finished lunch, but their teacher hasn't.

explanation.heading: Do not leave a positive contraction alone
explanation.body: Positive contractions such as I'm, she's and they've cannot normally stand by themselves at the end of these short answers or contrasts. Say Yes, I am, not Yes, I'm. Say but he is, not but he's. Negative contractions like isn't and won't can stand alone.

left.label: Present simple
left.example: I enjoy cycling, but my brother doesn’t.

right.label: Past simple
right.example: I enjoyed the concert, but my brother didn’t.
right.note: Didn’t replaces didn’t enjoy the concert.

left.label: Positive
left.note: The full positive auxiliary is needed at the end.

right.label: Negative
right.note: A negative contraction can end the reply.

examples.sentence: Our neighbour grows herbs, but we don't.
I haven't finished the puzzle, but Theo has.
examples.note: Has stands for has finished the puzzle.

examples.sentence: The shop was open this morning, but the café wasn't.
examples.note: Wasn’t refers to the café not being open.
Can answers the same modal question.

examples.sentence: 'Will the buses run tomorrow?' 'Yes, they will.'
examples.note: Will is the matching auxiliary in the short answer.

commonMistakes.why: An affirmative contracted auxiliary cannot stand alone.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Leo plays chess, but his sisters doesn't.
commonMistakes.correct: Leo plays chess, but his sisters don't.
commonMistakes.why: The plural subject sisters takes do not / don’t.

commonMistakes.incorrect: We went to the exhibition yesterday, but Max doesn't.
commonMistakes.correct: We went to the exhibition yesterday, but Max didn't.
commonMistakes.why: A finished past action uses did or didn’t.
A will question needs will in the short answer.

studyTips: Find the auxiliary in the first clause or question, then reuse the right form in your short reply.
Check both tense and subject when choosing do, does, did, have, has, was or were.
Remember: positive short replies end with the full auxiliary (Yes, I am), but negative contractions are fine (No, I’m not).

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast: “My cousins don’t eat fish, but I ___.”
exercises.feedback: Do replaces eat fish in a present simple statement with the subject I.

exercises.prompt: Choose the short answer: “Will your flatmate be home tonight?” “Yes, she ___.”
exercises.feedback: A question with will takes will in the affirmative short answer.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct response: “Did Emma finish the report yesterday?” “No, she ___.”
exercises.feedback: The past simple question Did ...? takes didn’t in a negative short answer.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast: “My friend can’t ride a bicycle yet, but I ___.”
exercises.feedback: Can replaces can ride a bicycle and matches the modal in the earlier clause.

exercises.prompt: Complete using the negative present simple auxiliary: “My brother enjoys jazz, but I ___.”
exercises.feedback: Don’t replaces don’t enjoy jazz after the subject I.

exercises.prompt: Complete using the negative past form of be: “We were ready at eight, but our taxi ___.”
exercises.feedback: The singular taxi takes was not to contrast with were ready.

exercises.prompt: Complete with one affirmative auxiliary: “I haven’t visited Madrid, but my sister ___.”
exercises.feedback: Has stands for has visited Madrid and agrees with my sister.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the matching auxiliary: “We won’t be late, but the other team definitely ___.”
exercises.feedback: Will stands for will be late and contrasts with won’t.

exercises.prompt: Correct the final short form in this sentence: “The green box isn’t heavy, but the blue box’s.”
acceptedAnswers: The green box isn’t heavy, but the blue box is.
exercises.feedback: In this contrast, a positive is must be written in full when it stands alone.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: “Maya likes swimming, but her brothers doesn’t.”
acceptedAnswers: Maya likes swimming, but her brothers don’t.
exercises.feedback: Her brothers is plural, so use don’t, not doesn’t.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: “I didn’t visit the gallery, but Paul does.”
acceptedAnswers: I didn’t visit the gallery, but Paul did.
exercises.feedback: The first clause is past simple, so the contrasting short verb must be did.

exercises.prompt: Correct the reply in this exchange: “Are your neighbours at home? Yes, they do.”
acceptedAnswers: Are your neighbours at home? Yes, they are.
exercises.feedback: The question begins with are, so the short answer must use are.

speakingExercises.prompt: You are ready. Reply to “Are you ready?” with a positive short answer only.
speakingExercises.feedback: The question uses are with you, and the positive reply uses am with I.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your grandparents do not live in this town. Reply to “Do your grandparents live here?” with a negative short answer only.
speakingExercises.feedback: A present simple question about they takes don’t in the negative reply.

speakingExercises.prompt: Leo emailed you yesterday. Reply to “Did Leo email you yesterday?” with a positive short answer only.
speakingExercises.feedback: Did is the past simple auxiliary that answers the question.

speakingExercises.prompt: Mia has finished her homework, but Ben has not. Say one sentence beginning 'Mia has finished her homework, but Ben' and end with the negative auxiliary.
acceptedAnswers: Mia has finished her homework, but Ben hasn't.
Mia has finished her homework, but Ben has not.
speakingExercises.feedback: Hasn't replaces hasn't finished his homework without repeating the verb phrase.

speakingExercises.prompt: Shorten 'I like tea, but Sam does not like tea' without repeating 'like tea'. Keep the start 'I like tea, but Sam'.
acceptedAnswers: I like tea, but Sam doesn't.
I like tea, but Sam does not.
speakingExercises.feedback: Doesn't replaces doesn't like tea in a present simple contrast with Sam.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friend asks, 'Has your father booked the tickets?' He has booked them. Give only a positive short answer using 'he'.
speakingExercises.feedback: A present perfect question with has takes has in the positive short answer; do not use he's.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your friends are hungry. Someone asks, 'Are your friends hungry?' Correct the wrong reply 'Yes, they're' by saying only a grammatical positive short answer using 'they'.
speakingExercises.feedback: An affirmative auxiliary at the end of a short answer must be full: Yes, they are, not Yes, they're.

speakingExercises.prompt: Two dogs can swim, but your cat cannot. Say one sentence beginning 'The dogs can swim, but my cat' and finish with only the negative modal.
acceptedAnswers: The dogs can swim, but my cat can't.
The dogs can swim, but my cat cannot.
speakingExercises.feedback: Can't or cannot replaces can't swim, while can remains unchanged after the plural subject dogs.

listeningExercises.audioText: I don't drink coffee, but my partner does.
listeningExercises.feedback: Does stands for drinks coffee and refers to the speaker’s partner.

listeningExercises.audioText: Nina can drive, but her brother can't.
listeningExercises.prompt: Who is unable to drive, according to the speaker?
listeningExercises.feedback: Can’t signals that Nina’s brother is unable to drive.

listeningExercises.audioText: The library isn't open today, but the bookshop is.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single auxiliary at the very end of the spoken sentence.
listeningExercises.feedback: The final is stands for is open, with no need to repeat open.

listeningExercises.audioText: Oscar didn't finish the race, but his sister did.
listeningExercises.feedback: Did stands for finished the race; the sister finished, but Oscar did not.

listeningExercises.audioText: The tickets haven't arrived yet, but the hotel confirmation has.
listeningExercises.feedback: Has means has arrived and refers to the hotel confirmation, not the tickets.

listeningExercises.audioText: We will take the train tomorrow, but Daniel won't because he has a car.
listeningExercises.prompt: Who plans to travel by train?
choices: The speaker's group, but not Daniel.
listeningExercises.feedback: Won't replaces won't take the train. Daniel is travelling differently from the speaker's group.

listeningExercises.audioText: I can't carry this heavy bag, but my brother can.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the single auxiliary at the end that avoids repeating the action.
listeningExercises.feedback: Can stands for can carry this heavy bag and contrasts with can't.

listeningExercises.audioText: The shops were open this morning, but the museum wasn't.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the negative past form of 'be' heard at the end.
listeningExercises.feedback: Wasn't stands for was not open, matching the singular museum and past time.
